questions.stem: Which of the following do not synthesise relaxin during pregnancy? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
Relaxin is not synthesised by the fetal adrenal gland in a pregnant woman. It is synthesised by corpus luteum, decidua and placenta.
Relaxin is a placental protein hormone. Plasma levels peak between 8 and 12 weeks of gestation and decline thereafter to lower levels that persist until term.
[[IMG:2]]
Functions of relaxin are:
Relaxation of myometrium and quiescence of early pregnancy
Enhancement of the glomerular filtration rate
Endometrial vascular remodelling by inducing secretion of VEGF

questions.stem: Which among the given features is not a major physiological change in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Among the given features hypothyroidism is not a major physiological change in pregnancy.
The  -subunits of hCG and TSH are identical. An increase in hCG during pregnancy stimulates thyroid and leads to a decrease in TSH levels. The thyroid undergoes enlargement and boosts the production of hormones. This is accompanied by increased production of thyroid-binding globulin(TBG). All these changes increase total T4 and T3 in the first trimester. But the physiologically important free T4 and T3 levels remain unchanged. Hence, physiologically pregnant women remain euthyroid.
Option A: Normal pregnancy is characterized by insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia. Human placental lactogen(hPL) secreted during pregnancy, helps in adaptation to fetal energy requirements. Insulin resistance causes prolonged hyperglycemia and glucose flow to the fetus. It also favours protein synthesis. To counterbalance the increased insulin resistance and prevent maternal hyperglycemia, maternal insulin levels are increased.
Option B: By the 3rd trimester, there is an increase in the maternal basal metabolic rate by 10 to 20% in comparison to a nonpregnant woman.
Option D: During normal pregnancy, mean arterial pressure and vascular resistance decrease, while blood volume and cardiac output rate increase. This helps in meeting metabolic demands of the enlarged uterus, provide nutrients to rapidly growing placenta and fetus, safeguard mother against the effects of parturition-associated blood loss.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman with diabetes mellitus is advised to increase her insulin dose as pregnancy is characterised by insulin resistance. Which of the following is not implicated in this phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
hCG is not implicated in insulin resistance during pregnancy.
As the fetus is dependant on maternal glucose for sustenance, the blood glucose levels are maintained at a high level in the mother. In response to this, the insulin level in the mother increases, which reduces the maternal blood glucose. To counteract this, the placenta secretes certain hormones which increase insulin resistance in the mother. This resistance is maximal between 24 to 28 weeks.
Hormones increasing insulin resistance include:
Human placental lactogen - Increases lipolysis and liberation of free fatty acids
Progesterone and estrogen
Placental growth hormone - Major determinant of maternal insulin resistance after mid-pregnancy
[[IMG:1]]
Cortisol
Prolactin

questions.stem: Which of the following changes are not seen in the renal system during pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Serum creatinine levels decrease during normal pregnancy from a mean of 0.7 mg/dL to 0.5 mg/dL.
Physiological changes in the renal system during pregnancy include:
Increase in:
Renal blood flow(+80%)
GFR(+50%)
Creatinine clearance
Glucosuria
Decrease in:
Plasma osmolality
Creatinine
Uric acid
Na/K/Cl
Anatomical changes in the renal system during pregnancy include:
Both kidneys enlarge by 1 cm
Hydroureter and hydronephrosis - More common on the right side due to dextrorotation of the uterus
Congestion of the bladder causing decreased bladder capacity
Increased bladder pressure and intraurethral pressure

questions.stem: Which of the following is increased during pregnancy? [[IMG:1]]
options: Total oxygen carrying capacity of blood
questions.explanation:
The total oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood increases during pregnancy.
During pregnancy, there is an increase in total haemoglobin (Hb) resulting in increased total oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. However, there is a relative decrease in Hb concentration (hematocrit) due to a greater increase in plasma volume. This decreases oxygen-carrying capacity per unit volume of blood.
Maternal iron stores are not sufficient to meet the increased demand during pregnancy and hence the serum iron and ferritin concentration falls.
The plasma volume expansion also lowers serum potassium.
[[IMG:2]]

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a physiological change seen in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Decrease in peripheral vascular resistance is a physiological change seen in pregnancy. Cardiovascular parameters that increase in pregnancy are:
Cardiac output
Stroke volume
Heart rate
Cardiovascular parameters that decrease in pregnancy are:
Peripheral vascular resistance (due to smooth muscle relaxation by progesterone)
Both diastolic BP and systolic BP (decrease in DBP > SBP)
Mean arterial BP
Artery venous O2 gradient

questions.stem: A primigravida presents in the 2nd trimester complaining that her slippers do not fit anymore. On examination, her pulse is 88/min and blood pressure is 130/84mm Hg. You note bilateral pitting edema up to the level of ankles. What would you advise her?
questions.explanation:
The clinical features are suggestive of physiological edema during pregnancy for which the most appropriate treatment is bed rest.
It occurs due to increased venous pressure of the inferior extremities by the gravid uterus pressing on the common iliac veins.
Features of physiological edema in pregnancy are:
Slight degree of ankle edema
Usually confined to one leg, more commonly the right leg
Not associated with any other features of preeclampsia (like BP>140/90mm Hg, proteinuria)
Disappears with rest
Other cardiac, renal and hematological pathologies are absent

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a physiological change seen during pregnancy?
options: Pulmonary blood flow is increased by 2,500 mL/min
Blood flow to the skin decreases to 300 mL/min
Blood flow to the uterus increases to 750 mL/min
Renal blood flow increases by 400 mL/min
questions.explanation:
The blood flow to the skin and mucous membranes increases during pregnancy to a maximum of 500 mL/min by the 36th week. Symptoms experienced during pregnancy such as increased heat sensation, sweating or having a stuffy nose can be explained by the increased blood flow.
Regional distribution of blood flow during pregnancy:
Uterine blood flow - increased from 50 mL/min in the non-pregnant state to about 750 mL near term.
[[IMG:1]]
Pulmonary blood flow - increased by 2,500 mL/min.
Renal blood flow - increases by 400 mL/min at 16th week and remains at this level till term.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old primigravida presents to the antenatal clinic at 30 weeks of gestation. During examination, which of the following cardiovascular findings would not be a cause for alarm? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
S3 is normally heard during pregnancy.
The third heart sound (S3) occurs due to rapid diastolic filling in hypervolemic states such as pregnancy, anemia or thyrotoxicosis. Hypervolemia is a normal physiological change during pregnancy.
The auscultation of a fixed split S2, fourth heart sound (S4) or a pericardial knock are suggestive of cardiac pathology.

questions.stem: Which of the following coagulation factors are increased in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
All clotting factors increase in pregnancy except factors XI and XIII. Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state with physiological changes such as:
All clotting factors are increased (except factors XI and XIII)
Fibrinogen levels are also increased
The viscosity of blood decreases due to hemodilution
Clotting time and bleeding time is unaffected
The most common cause of decreased platelet count in pregnancy is benign gestational thrombocytopenia. This is due to hemodilution and increased platelet consumption and the women are generally asymptomatic.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old primigravida at 38 weeks of gestation presents to the antenatal clinic with complaints of dizziness on lying down for the past one week. She feels better on sitting up or turning to the side. What is the cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The clinical features are suggestive of supine hypotension syndrome due to inferior vena caval compression.
During late pregnancy, the gravid uterus produces a compression effect on the inferior vena cava (IVC) when the patient is in the supine position. To compensate, there will be an opening up of the collaterals of paravertebral and azygous veins.
When collaterals fail to open, venous return of the heart is reduced leading to hypotension, tachycardia, and syncope. The normal blood pressure is quickly restored by turning the patient to lateral position.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding the sensitivity of uterine musculature?
options: Enhanced by both estrogen and progesterone
Enhanced by estrogen and inhibited by progesterone
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
The sensitivity of uterine musculature is enhanced by estrogen and inhibited by progesterone.
Estrogen stimulates the synthesis of myometrial contractile proteins through cAMP. This increases the excitability of uterine muscles and the frequency of action potentials.
Progesterone decreases the frequency and intensity of uterine contractions. This helps to prevent the expulsion of the implanted ovum. However, it increases the amplitude of contraction.

questions.stem: [[IMG:1]] A pregnant woman has cramps in her legs. What will you suggest her to relieve the pain?
options: Extend knee and plantar flex foot
Flex knee and plantar flex foot
questions.explanation:
Extension at the knee joint and dorsiflexion at the ankle joint helps in stretching the calf muscles which relieves the pain.
Leg cramps are minor ailments during pregnancy mostly due to a deficiency of diffusible serum calcium or elevation of serum phosphorus. Management includes massaging the leg, stretching exercises, application of local heat, and supplementation of vitamin B1 and calcium.

questions.stem: Theca lutein cysts are not associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Theca lutein cysts are not seen in hyperprolactinemia.
Theca-lutein cysts are benign ovarian lesions resulting from exaggerated physiological follicle stimulation. They are usually associated with markedly elevated serum levels of hCG.
Theca lutein cysts are found in association with:
Large placenta
Diabetes
Anti-D alloimmunization
Multifetal gestations
Fetal hydrops
Gestational trophoblastic disease - Molar pregnancy
Reduced hCG clearance - Chronic renal failure
They may also be found in normal pregnancy due to an exaggerated response of the ovaries to normal circulating levels of hCG.

questions.stem: In which trimester does acute fatty liver manifest most commonly during pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) occurs most commonly in the third trimester or early postpartum period.
[[IMG:1]]
Risk factors include Pre-eclampsia/HELLP syndrome, male fetus, previous history of AFLP, and multiple gestations.
AFLP (acute yellow atrophy or acute fatty metamorphosis) is the most common cause of acute liver failure in pregnancy. It usually occurs in the later stages of pregnancy, particularly in
the third trimester. It occurs due to fetal deficiency of long-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase (LCHAD) or poor placental mitochondrial function.
The patients present with persistent nausea and vomiting, progressive jaundice, and epigastric pain. Features like acute hemolysis, hypoglycemia, hypertension, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, and edema can also be present. Symptoms may progress to fulminant hepatic failure with encephalopathy, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and death.
Liver function tests such as AST, ALT, and serum bilirubin levels are raised. Hypofibrinogenemia, hypocholesterolemia, and prolonged clotting time can be seen. An elevated d-dimer is
seen. Microscopy reveals a characteristic microvesicular fatty infiltration.
The condition worsens till delivery after which the hepatic dysfunction resolves. A trial of labor by induction or delivery by Cesarean is done. Intensive supportive measures including blood transfusion should be provided.
The clinical and laboratory findings of acute liver diseases in pregnancy are as follows:
The condition worsens till delivery after which the hepatic dysfunction resolves. Appropriate management is immediate termination of pregnancy irrespective of gestational age by induction or delivery by Cesarean (for obstetric reasons) is done. Intensive supportive measures including blood transfusion should be provided.

questions.stem: What does the term 'placental sign' denote? [[IMG:1]]
options: Alteration of fetal heart rate on pressing the head into the pelvis
Spotting on the expected date of period in early months of pregnancy
Permanent lengthening of the cord in 3rd stage of labor
Slight gush of bleeding in 3rd stage of labor
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:2]]
Spotting on the expected date of menstruation in the early months of pregnancy is known as placental sign.
Cyclic bleeding may occur up to 12 weeks of pregnancy until the decidual space is obliterated by the fusion of decidua parietalis with decidua capsularis. The bleeding is usually scanty and lasts for a shorter duration than in a regular menstrual cycle.
Option A: Slowing of the fetal heart rate (FHR) on pressing the head down into the pelvis is suggestive of placenta previa (especially of posterior type) and is called Stallworthy’s sign. The fetal heart rate recovers as soon as the pressure is released.
Options C and D: Permanent lengthening of the cord and slight gush of bleeding in 3rd stage of labor are suggestive of separation of the placenta.

options: It uses cell-free circulating fetal DNA in the maternal serum
It is used for the diagnosis of trisomy 13, 18 and 21
It can be performed after 10 weeks of gestation
It is done after the routine first trimester ultrasound assessment
questions.explanation:
Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) is used for the screening of trisomy 13, 18 and 21 and Turner's syndrome. It is not a diagnostic test.
It is a novel genetic test that uses cell-free circulating fetal DNA in the maternal serum for screening of chromosomal anomalies.
DNA from the fetus is found circulating in the maternal blood in two forms - either inside the intact fetal cells or as cell-free DNA from the breakdown of placental fetal cells. In NIPT, the cell-free chromosome fragments are measured and the quantitative differences from normal fetuses are noted.
NIPT can be performed after 10 weeks of gestation and is recommended after the routine
first-trimester ultrasound assessment in high-risk pregnancies or if either 1st or 2nd-trimester screening becomes positive. Its disadvantage is that it is very expensive and it can be used for screening of only a few chromosomal anomalies such as trisomy 13, 18, and 21 and it doesn't analyse the entire karyotype.

Amniocentesis is a diagnostic test for amniotic fluid AFP measurement. It was once considered the standard for the diagnosis of open neural tube disorders but has been replaced in most centers by targeted sonography.
Defects in fetal integuments, such as ventral wall and neural tube defects, permit fetal AFP to leak into the amnionic fluid. This results in increased MSAFP levels. This is detected on screening performed from 15 to 20 weeks of gestation.

questions.explanation:
The maternal serum AFP screening is generally performed from 15-20 weeks of gestation. Hence, it is detected in this period.
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is the major serum protein in the embryo and fetus. It is produced by the yolk sac and fetal liver.
Option B: Diabetic patients have low levels of AFP.
Option C: Gestational age influences the MSAFP levels. The maternal serum concentration increases by approximately 15% per week during the second trimester.
Option D: At about 13 weeks of gestation, the AFP concentration in the fetal serum and amniotic fluid are highest, after which it declines. Conversely, AFP is found in steadily increasing quantities in maternal serum after 12 weeks.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman brings her son to the hospital for routine immunization. While awaiting his turn, she realizes that her seat is stained with blood. She is rushed to the nearby antenatal clinic. Pulse - 96/min, BP - 110/80 mmHg. Vaginal bleeding is noted and her NST is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis? [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]]
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:3]]

The given clinical scenario along with the NST showing a sinusoidal pattern point towards a diagnosis of vasa previa.
Vasa previa is a condition where fetal vessels travel within the membranes and overlie the cervical os. Hence, there can be bleeding during cervical dilatation or membrane rupture.
Fetal mortality is high due to fetal exsanguination. When bleeding is present in vasa previa, an emergency cesarean section is indicated.
Causes of sinusoidal pattern on NST include:
Severe fetal anemia - Rh isoimmunisation, vasa previa, fetomaternal hemorrhage, or twin to twin transfusion
Opioids - meperidine, morphine, alphaprodine, butorphanol
Amnionitis
Fetal distress
Umbilical cord occlusion.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with 2 months of amenorrhea and a positive UPT. On ultrasound examination, all of the following are assessed except . [[IMG:1]]

Fetal number, including amnionicity and chorionicity of multifetal gestations
Embryonic/fetal cardiac activity
Maternal uterus, adnexa, and cul-de-sac
Fetal nuchal translucency.

questions.stem: A primigravida presents to the antenatal clinic for the first time at 18 weeks of amenorrhea. She does not remember her LMP and no ultrasound scans were done in the first trimester. questions.explanation:

[[IMG:1]]
BPD is measured in the transthalamic view, at the level of the thalamus and cavum septum pellucidum (CSP). It is measured from the outer edge of the skull in the near field to the inner edge of the skull in the far field.

questions.stem: What is the normal range of femur length to abdominal circumference ratio?
questions.explanation:
The normal range for the femoral length (FL) to abdominal circumference (AC) ratio is 20-24 percent.
Low FL/AC (< 16) ratio suggests a lethal skeletal dysplasia, particularly if other skeletal abnormalities are present.

questions.stem: A woman presents at 33-weeks of gestation and the umbilical artery Doppler imaging shows the following finding. What is the next step of management? [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]]
options: Terminate the pregnancy at 34 weeks of gestation
questions.explanation:
The umbilical artery Doppler depicts reversal of end-diastolic flow or REDF (waves appearing below the baseline) which is seen in intrauterine growth restriction. As the period of gestation has exceeded 32 weeks, the pregnancy can be terminated.
In case of absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF), the waves just touch the baseline, but don't appear below it. This suggests a fetal compromise, hence the pregnancy is terminated by C-section if >34 weeks.

Reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF) suggests impending fetal death, hence the pregnancy is terminated by C-section if >32 weeks.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding the first-trimester ultrasound?
options: A gestational sac can first be seen 4 weeks after LMP
Accuracy of USG dating decreases after the 1st trimester
Yolk sac is the first sign of pregnancy on USG
A normal gestational sac implants in the midline of the endometrial cavity
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
The accuracy of determining gestational age using ultrasound is the highest in the first trimester and decreases afterwards.
Option A: Gestational sac is reliably seen at 5 weeks of gestation on transvaginal sonography(TVS).
Option C: The first sign of pregnancy seen on sonography is the gestational sac. Visualisation of the yolk sac within the gestational sac confirms an intrauterine location for pregnancy.
Option D: A normal gestational sac implants eccentrically in the endometrium, whereas a pseudosac is seen in the midline of the endometrial cavity.

questions.stem: What is the ideal time for nuchal translucency evaluation?
questions.explanation:
Nuchal translucency evaluation, a component of first-trimester aneuploidy screening, is done between 11-14 weeks.
It represents the maximum thickness of the subcutaneous translucent area between the skin and soft tissue, overlying the fetal spine, at the back of the neck. When the nuchal translucency is increased, the risk of fetal aneuploidy and structural anomalies such as heart defects is significantly elevated.
First trimester aneuploidy screening combines two maternal serum analytes and a sonographic measurement:
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
Pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A)
Nuchal translucency (NT)
It is performed between 11 and 14 weeks of gestation. In cases of fetal Down syndrome, the first-trimester serum-free -hCG level is higher and the PAPP-A level is lower. With trisomy 18 and trisomy 13, levels of both analytes are lower.
Note: Nuchal fold is a normal fold of skin seen at the back of the fetal neck during the second trimester of pregnancy. Increased nuchal fold thickness is associated with fetal aneuploidy.

questions.stem: A doctor tells a 31-year-old woman, who is 20 weeks pregnant, that her baby has a developmental defect. She has come to you for a second opinion. The following USG finding is seen. Identify the defect. [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]]
questions.explanation:
The given ultrasound image shows an open defect in the calvaria and skin leading to the exposure of the cranial neural tube. This is consistent with the diagnosis of anencephaly.
Anencephaly results from incomplete closure of the neural tube. It is one of the earliest detectable congenital defects that can be detected as early as 10 to 11 weeks of gestation. Screening can also be done by serum estimation of maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP). The following are the radiological signs seen in anencephaly.
Frog eye sign - Absence of cranial calvaria, prominent orbits thereby resembling the face of a frog.
Shower cap sign - The absence of the cranium could lead to the protrusion of a disorganized mass of brain tissue. This resembles a shower cap giving rise to a characteristic triangular facial appearance.
[[IMG:3]]
[[IMG:4]]
Neural-tube defects can be prevented with pre-conceptional supplementation of folic acid. A dose of 4 mg daily is recommended in subsequent pregnancies.
The frog eye and showercap signs are shown below:

Option B: Omphalocele is a midline anterior abdominal wall defect through which the solid abdominal viscera and/or bowel may herniate. The extruded abdominal contents are covered in a sac. Given below is an ultrasound image of the fetus suggestive of an omphalocele (asterix).
Cystic hygroma is a congenital multiloculated lymphatic lesion that is classically found in the left posterior triangle of the neck. It occurs as a result of sequestration or obstruction of developing lymph vessels. This defect can be picked up in a first-trimester ultrasound. The images below show the MRI and USG appearance of cystic hygroma, respectively:
[[IMG:6]]
[[IMG:7]]

Encephalocele is caused due to defects in the skull through which the meninges and/or neural tissue herniate. The squamous part of the occipital bone is the most frequently affected bone.

questions.stem: What is Robert's sign?
questions.explanation:
Robert's sign is a gas shadow in the fetal heart. It is seen in fetal demise in utero and may appear as early as 12 hours.

Absent fetal heartbeat
Absent fetal movements
Occasional findings

Uncommon findings

questions.stem: A pregnant diabetic woman presents for a routine antenatal visit during the third trimester. During the evaluation, you perform obstetrical Doppler imaging. Which among the following would indicate fetal compromise?
options: Increased pulsatalilty index in umbilical artery
questions.explanation:
Absent end diastolic flow indicates fetal compromise in Doppler. Umbilical artery vessels:
They are characterized by forward low-resistance flow.
As gestation increases, there is a gradual fall in all the resistance indices so the amount of forward diastolic flow increases.
S/D ratio decreases as the period of gestation increases. Abnormal flow patterns in umbilical artery:
Reduced end-diastolic flow - Uteroplacental insufficiency (systolic/diastolic ratio increases)
Absent end-diastolic flow - Fetal compromise (hence pregnancy is terminated by cesarean section if >34 weeks)
Reverse end-diastolic flow - Impending death (pregnancy is terminated irrespective of gestational age)
Doppler of the middle cerebral artery helps in detecting fetal anemia. Increased fetal diastolic flow in the middle cerebral artery with absent diastolic flow in the aorta implies fetal acidemia.

questions.stem: What are the cardinal movements of labour? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The cardinal movements of labour are engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, external rotation, expulsion.
(Mnemonic: Every Day FIRE Raises Extremely)
Every: Engagement
Day: Descent
F: Flexion
IR: Internal rotation
E: Extension
Raises: external Rotation
Extremely: Expulsion
The most common presentation is cephalic and presenting part is vertex. Head enters the pelvis through transverse diameter majorly and left occipito transverse is the commonest fetal position. Internal rotation of fetal head occurs at the level of ischial spine. In a vertex delivery, the baby's head is delivered by extension and in a breech delivery, the baby's head is delivered by flexion.
The best time to give episotomy is after crowning has occured.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a prerequisite for internal rotation of the fetal head for a woman in labor?

Favorable shape at mid-pelvic plane
Tone of the levator ani muscles

questions.stem: Which of the following is part of the WHO guidelines for the management of second stage of labor?
options: Manual support to perineum to maintain flexion of head
Never give warm compress to the perineum
questions.explanation:
The practice of guarding the perineum during delivery of the fetal head is part of the WHO management guidelines for the second stage of labor.
The fingers of one hand support the perineum, while the second hand applies pressure to the fetal head to control the speed of crowning. The advantage of this is to prevent perineal tears.
The second stage of labor begins with full dilatation of the cervix and ends with the delivery of the fetus.
The main events include the descent of the fetus (bearing down by the mother, uterine contractions), cardinal movements of labor, and delivery of the fetus.
[[IMG:1]]
Management of the second stage of labor:
The most common position used is the dorsal position with the hips flexed, knees flexed and abduction of the thighs. WHO recommends any position of choice including the upright position.
WHO recommendations for the prevention of perineal tears include warm compresses to the perineum, perineal massage, guarding the perineum, and modified Ritgen's maneuver.
Modified Ritgen's maneuver: A sterile towel or pad is held in one hand and placed over the perineum; the other hand applies gentle downward pressure on the occiput to promote flexion and controlled delivery of the head (ensuring the smallest diameter of the head passes through the outlet). Once the occiput is born–with gentle pressure, the head is extended–forehead, nose, and mouth are then delivered.
WHO doesn't recommend fundal pressure and routine episiotomy. Other options:
Option A: A liberal or routine episiotomy is discouraged. Episiotomy is indicated in cases of:
Shoulder dystocia
Breech delivery
Fetal macrosomia
Operative vaginal deliveries
Persistent occiput posterior positions
Option C: Manual techniques, such as massage or application of warm compresses, are recommended for healthy pregnant women requesting pain relief during labor.
Option D: The position that is most comfortable to the mother i.e. upright/squatting position is encouraged. This position gives:
less discomfort and difficulty in bearing down
less labor pain
less perineal/vaginal trauma and wound infections

questions.explanation:
True labor pain is not relieved by enema and sedatives. It is characterized by the following:
[[IMG:1]]
Painful uterine contractions at regular intervals
The frequency of contractions increases gradually
The intensity and duration of contractions increase progressively
Associated with 'show'- extrusion of the mucus plug that had previously filled the cervical canal during pregnancy
Progressive effacement and dilatation of the cervix
Progressive descent of the presenting part
Formation of the 'bag of forewaters' i.e., bulging fluid-filled amniotic membrane presenting in front of the fetal head
Not relieved by enema or sedatives
False labour pain is seen more in primigravidae than in parous women. It usually appears prior to the onset of true labor pain by 1 or 2 weeks in primigravidae and by a few days in multiparae.
Such pains are probably due to stretching of the cervix and lower uterine segment with consequent irritation of the neighboring ganglia.
Features | True labour pains | False labour pain s
Cervical dilatation and efface ment | Present | Absent
Pain | Lower abdomen and back, ra diating to thighs | Lower abdomen only
Show | Present | Absent
Bag of water | Formed | Absent
Relief with enema | No | Yes

questions.stem: You notice the gynecology resident administer the nerve block seen in the image before performing an episiotomy. Which nerve roots are blocked? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The nerve roots blocked in pudendal nerve block are S2,3,4. It is blocked just above the tip of the ischial spine by piercing the sacrospinous ligament.
Pudendal nerve block can be used for:
Analgesia in the second stage of labor
Episiotomy repair
Pelvic floor relaxation for outlet instrument delivery
Minor procedures of the lower vagina and perineum
Perineal analgesia prior to application of vacuum/forceps
Pudendal block does not impact the cervix or upper vagina. It is ineffective for pain relief associated with uterine manipulation such as manual extraction of the placenta.
[[IMG:2]]

questions.stem: [[IMG:1]] Paracervical block relieves pain from all except:
questions.explanation:
Pain from the lower third of the vagina is relieved by pudendal block, not paracervical block.
Paracervical block relieves the pain of uterine contractions and cervical dilatation. It also relieves pain from upper third of the vagina. It is not useful at the time of episiotomy as the lower part of the vagina is not anesthetized.
Note: Paracervical block is no longer considered safe as it causes fetal bradycardia. Epidural analgesia is preferred when complete relief of pain is needed throughout labour.

questions.stem: All of the following are indications for early clamping of cord in a new born baby except:
questions.explanation:
Postdated pregnancy is not an indication for early cord clamping. Early cord clamping is indicated in:
Birth asphyxia
Rh isoimmunization
Diabetic mother
The benefits of delayed cord clamping for up to 60 seconds is an increase in total body iron stores, expand blood volume and a decrease in anemia incidence in the neonate.
On the other hand, delayed cord clamping can lead to a higher hemoglobin concentration, which increases risks for hyperbilirubinemia and extended hospitalization for neonatal phototherapy. Delayed cord clamping can also hinder timely neonatal resuscitation.
According to AIIMS Protocols in Neonatology, in uncomplicated preterm birth, delayed cord clamping should be attempted. This is done for a minimum time of 60 seconds after delivery for preterm infants not requiring immediate resuscitation after birth. It states that DCC must be done even if the mother has an HIV infection. But as per the NACO guidelines, early cord clamping is advised.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a sign of placental separation in stage 3 of parturition of a pregnant woman?
questions.explanation:
Lengthening of the umbilical cord is seen in placental separation. Signs of placental separation:
The uterus becomes globular, firm, and ballottable (earliest sign to appear)
Schroeder's sign - Slight rise of fundal height as the separated placenta comes down in the lower segment and uterus rests over it
Slight suprapubic bulging due to separated placenta distending the lower segment.
Kustner's sign - On pushing, the uterus cephalad with a hand on the abdomen, the cord no longer recedes
[[IMG:1]]
A sudden gush of blood
Permanent lengthening of cord
Note: Schroeder's ring is a constriction ring/contraction ring formed due to incoordinate uterine action.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false regarding the modified WHO partogram?
options: Right side of alert line indicates immediate referral to First Referral Unit (FRU)
Alert and action line are separated by a difference of 4 hours
Each small square in partogram is equal to 1 hour
Partograph recording should be started once the cervical dilatation reaches 4 cm
questions.explanation: Each small square in a modified WHO partogram is equal to 30 minutes. Each small square in a composite WHO partogram is equal to 1 hour.

questions.stem: Identify the following instrument commonly used in obstetrics. [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]]
questions.explanation:
The instrument given in the picture is episiotomy scissors. The angulation in the scissor is to prevent the extension of pelvic tears into the anal margins and obstetric anal sphincter injuries / complete perineal tears.
Complications of episiotomy:
They can be immediate or remote.
Immediate complications include an extension of the incision into the rectum, vulval hematoma, wound dehiscence and injury to anal sphincter.
Remote complications include dyspareunia, chances of perineal lacerations in subsequent labor and scar endometriosis (rare).
Mayo scissors are long and stout scissors. They can be blunt-tipped/pointed tip/straight or curved. Straight mayo scissors are designed for cutting body tissues near the surface of a wound. They are also used to cut sutures and are also known as suture-cutting scissors.
Curved mayo scissors allow much deeper penetration into the wound and are used to cut thick tissues such as those found in the uterus, muscles, breast, and foot. Mayo scissors used for dissection are placed in tissue with the tips closed. The scissors are then opened so that the tips open and spread out the tissue during the dissection process.
[[IMG:3]]
[[IMG:4]]
[[IMG:5]]

questions.stem: A nursing assistant posted in the obstetric care unit was asked to monitor the progress of labour. After how much dilatation of the cervix, should she start the documentation?
questions.explanation:
The WHO Labour Care Guide begins the documentation of labour progression at 5 cm of cervical dilatation.
The WHO Labour Care Guide is a tool designed to help health personnel involved in labour care. It aims to
Guide the monitoring and help in the documentation of the progress of labour.
Guide the health professionals to offer supportive care throughout labour.
Assist doctors in promptly identifying and addressing emerging labour complications.
Prevent the use of unnecessary interventions in labour.
Support audits and quality improvement.
The differences between the WHO-modified partograph and the latest WHO Labour Care Guide are tabulated below:
Note: Previously the answer to the question was 4 cm (according to the modified WHO patograph). However, this information is outdated, therefore the answer to this question has been revised per the latest WHO guidelines.
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
WHO modified partograph | WHO Labour Care Guide
Documentation of labour pro gression begins at4 cmof cerv ical dilatation. | Documentation of labour pro gression begins at5 cmof cerv ical dilatation.
Fixed1 cm/hour ‘alert’ and ‘ac tion’lines | Time-based cut-offsforeach c entimetreof cervical dilatatio n to guide the obstetrician to take action. For example, at 5 cm of cervical dilatation, if t here is no progress >6 hours, action needs to be taken.
Monitoring of labour is restri cted to thefirst stageonly. | Monitoring ofthe second stag e of labouris included
No section on supportive car e interventions | Addition of a section onsupp ortive careof the mother- lab our companionship, pain reli ef, oral fluid intake and postu re
Documentation ofstrength, d uration, and frequencyof uter ine contractions | Documentation ofonlythedur ation and frequency of uterin e contractions

questions.stem: A young woman delivered her baby on the way to the hospital. While examining her, you notice a perineal tear. This injury could have been prevented by all except: [[IMG:1]]
options: Slow delivery of the head in between contractions
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:2]]
Perineal injury cannot be prevented in normal labor by routine timely episiotomy. Routine episiotomy is associated with an increased incidence of disruption of anal sphincters and rectal tears.
Indications of episiotomy:
Shoulder dystocia
Breech delivery
Fetal macrosomia
Operative vaginal deliveries
Persistent occiput posterior positions Methods of prevention of perineal laceration:
Avoid delivery by early extension
Deliver head in between contractions
Perform timely episiotomy when indicated (not routine).

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of true cephalopelvic disproportion in India?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause of true cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD) in India is rickets.
The most common cause of true CPD in developing countries is vitamin D deficiency and rickets. In developed countries, it is trauma to the pelvis. It occurs due to pelvic dystocia (larger fetus and smaller pelvis).
Relative CPD is the most common type of CPD. It is caused due to fetal malposition
(occipitoposterior position/brow presentation).

questions.stem: You are monitoring uterine contractions in a term primigravida in labor. You find that the contractions are uncoordinated and the frequency is about 8 contractions every 10 minutes. Which of the following is incorrect regarding your finding?
options: It is common in nulliparous labour
Management includes wait and watch policy
questions.explanation:
The given clinical finding is suggestive of uterine tachysystole. Oxytocin administration is not beneficial here as it leads to hyperstimulation of the uterus.
Tachysystole (hypertonic uterine dysfunction):
The uterine contractions are uncoordinated and increased in frequency (>5 contractions in 10 minutes)
Contractions occur with an increase in the baseline tone without rest in between them
It is associated with late active phase dysfunction i.e., when the cervix is almost 7 cm dilated
The most common cause is occipito-posterior position. Hence, a wait and watch policy is adopted
It is more common in nulliparous females
Oxytocin administration leads to hyperstimulation of the uterus and is not recommended. Hypotonic uterine dysfunction:
[[IMG:1]]
Uterine contractions are inadequate
It is associated with early active phase
It is more common in nulliparous females.

questions.stem: A 37-week primigravida has mild labor pains for 20 hours and the cervix is persistently 1 cm dilated but non-effaced. What would be the appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of either false labor pain or prolonged latent phase. The appropriate management is to sedate the patient and wait.
False labor can be differentiated from the latent phase of labor by therapeutic rest i.e., the patient is sedated with morphine.
Augmentation with oxytocin is done only in those patients who even after therapeutic rest continue to be in prolonged latent phase.
There is no indication of cesarean section unless cephalopelvic disproportion is
present. Amniotomy is not useful and should be avoided in patients with prolonged latent phase.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old G3P2L2 woman presents to the ER with hypotension and severe abdominal pain. On examination, fetal parts are palpable over the abdomen. USG abdomen revealed a large uterine wall defect. Which of the following is not a feature of this condition? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of uterine rupture. Maternal tachycardia is seen in this condition.
Clinical features of uterine rupture:
Maternal tachycardia
Fetal bradycardia/absent fetal heart sounds
Hypotension
Abdominal tenderness
Palpable fetal parts on per abdomen examination
Bandl’s ring
Bleeding per vagina
Hematuria
Common causes of uterine rupture are previous caesarean delivery, myomectomy, silent rupture (in previous pregnancy), excess use of oxytocin, grand multipara, uterine overdistension, obstructed labour, difficult forceps delivery, placenta percreta

questions.stem: A young primigravida at 36 weeks of gestation came with complaints of decreased perception of fetal movements for the past 2 days. NST is non-reactive and on ultrasound fetal cardiac activity is absent. What will be the best management in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical picture is suggestive of intrauterine fetal death (IUFD). The best management for such cases at 36 weeks is waiting for spontaneous expulsion.
[[IMG:1]]
Forceps extraction is only necessary if spontaneous expulsion doesn't take place.
Artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) is not done due to the risk of infections. Cesarean section is avoided as far as possible in case of fetal death.
Waiting till term is not recommended in cases of uterine infections, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and psychological upset.

questions.stem: A G2P1L0 woman presents to OPD at 36 weeks of gestation for a routine visit. She mentions that she has a history of prior stillbirth at 37 weeks. What is the best time for delivery in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The best time for elective delivery in patients with a history of previous stillbirth is 39 weeks, either by induction or cesarean section.
The recommendations for the management of subsequent pregnancy after stillbirth is as follows:
Ultrasonographic screening for fetal growth restriction after 28 weeks
Kick counts starting from 28 weeks of gestation
Antepartum fetal surveillance starting at 32 weeks or 1-2 weeks earlier than prior stillbirth
Support and reassurance
Labor induction is suitable in such cases. Cesarean delivery is done for those with a contraindication to induction.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman presents with obstructed labor and is grossly dehydrated. Investigations reveal fetal demise. What will be the management? [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]]
questions.explanation:
The best management in the given clinical scenario is cesarean section.
Obstructive labor management involves administering intravenous fluids to correct dehydration, providing antibiotics to prevent infection, and promptly performing a cesarean section to relieve the obstruction. If the fetus is alive, an immediate cesarean section is typically performed.
Management of obstructed labor never involves a wait-and-watch approach or augmenting with oxytocin.
Clinical features of obstructed labor include maternal exhaustion, dehydration, tachycardia, tachypnea, genital sepsis, postpartum hemorrhage, and shock.
On P/A examination the upper uterine segment is tender and tonically contracted. The lower uterine segment is thin and stretched. A groove/depression is felt between the upper uterine segment and the lower uterine segment. This is called a Bandls ring.
Complications of obstructed labor include rupture of the uterus and vesicovaginal fistula.

questions.stem: The partogram of a 28 year old G2P1 is shown below. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
The above partogram shows a case of obstructed labour and management is caesarean section.
There is a secondary arrest of dilatation for >2 hours and arrest of descent for >1 hour. The patient has adequate uterine contractions as shown. The amniotic fluid is stained with meconium and there is fall in fetal heart rate which indicates that the baby is in distress.
[[IMG:1]]
There is no place for wait and watch and use of oxytocin to stimulate uterine contractions in obstructed labor.
Forceps can be applied only when the cervix is fully dilated and the head is low down.

questions.stem: After successful delivery of the baby, the obstetrician witnesses that the episiotomy performed has extended backwards beyond the perineal body. Which among the following structures is likely to be injured in this case?
questions.explanation:
External anal sphincter is the structure injured in an episiotomy extended posteriorly beyond the perineal body.
Perineal tear have been divided into four degrees:
First degree- laceration is restricted to the skin of the fourchette
Second degree- muscles of the perineal body are torn through
Third degree- the tear extends partially backward through the external sphincter of the anus
Fourth degree- the external anal sphincter is torn and anal mucosa is also involved
A central tear of the perineum is when the head penetrates first through the posterior vaginal wall, then through the perineal body and appears through the skin of the perineum. It usually occurs in patients with a contracted outlet.

questions.stem: A midwife is examining a pregnant woman in labour when she noticed that the cord is prolapsed. What should be the next immediate step of management? [[IMG:1]]
options: Gently replace the cord inside the vagina
Inform the doctor and shift to OT
Do vaginal examination and find the fetal presentation
questions.explanation:
In this scenario the midwife should put the pregnant women in a Trendelenburg position or in an exaggerated and elevated Sims’ position with a pillow or wedge under the hip or thigh.
Caesarean section is the recommended treatment of choice for cord prolapse. Prior to performing the procedure, several measures can be taken to alleviate cord compression. These measures involve:
Manually elevating the fetal presenting part using two fingers or the entire hand through the vagina
Positioning the patient in steep Trendelenburg, exaggerated Sim's position, or knee-chest position
Filling the bladder with 500–700 cc or more of saline (known as the Vagos method)
After the diagnosis of cord prolapse is made, it is crucial not to attempt cord replacement. Such attempts are not only ineffective but also result in the inevitable rupture of the membranes, leading to cord prolapse.

questions.stem: Abdominal examination of a 28-year-old primigravida, who is in the second stage of labour, reveals retraction ring between the active upper segment and the distended lower segment. Which would best describe this ring?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
Bandl's ring refers to pathological retraction ring. It is formed in cases of obstructed labour.
The upper segment of the uterus contracts and retracts vigourously in an attempt to overcome the obstruction while the lower segment dilates.
With each contraction there is myometrial shortening so that the actively contracting upper segment becomes progressively thicker and shorter. The passive lower segment is progressively stretched and becomes thinner.
The junction between the two segments stands out prominently as a pathological retraction ring.
Schroeder's constriction ring is formed due to incordinate uterine action when there is localized spastic contraction of a ring of circular muscle fibres of the uterus. It is formed due to injudicious use of oxytocin and premature rupture of membranes (PROM).
[[IMG:3]]
[[IMG:4]]
[[IMG:5]]

questions.stem: A 26-year-old term primigravida presents to the clinic for a regular check-up. On examination, uterus corresponds to term and head of the fetus is non-engaged. What is the most common cause for this finding?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause of non-engagement at term in a primigravida is deflexed head followed by cephalopelvic disproportion.
Non-engagement at the onset of active phase of labour is a risk factor for caesarean section.
The problems of prolonged labour are that the woman is exposed to high risk of infection, ketosis and obstructed labour while the fetus faces the danger of asphyxia and infection.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a cardinal movement occurring during labor? [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]]
questions.explanation:
Asynclitism is not a cardinal movement during labor.
Asynclitism refers to the position of a baby in the uterus such that the head of the baby is presenting first and is tilted to the shoulder. This causes the fetal head to no longer be in line with the birth canal.
Moderate degrees of asynclitism are the rule in normal labor. However, if severe, this condition is a common reason for cephalopelvic disproportion even with an otherwise normal sized pelvis.
Asynclitism can be of 2 types:
When the sagittal suture lies anteriorly, the posterior parietal bone becomes the leading presenting part and is called posterior asynclitism.
[[IMG:3]]
[[IMG:4]]
When the sagittal suture lies posteriorly, the anterior parietal bone becomes the leading presenting part and is called anterior asynclitism.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old primigravida is brought to the labour room in the latent phase of labor. How long will you wait till you declare her latent phase to be prolonged?
questions.explanation:
Latent phase is said to be prolonged in a primigravida if it lasts for more than 20 hours. Friedman defined prolonged latent phase as:
A nullipara who has not entered the active phase by 20 hours after the onset of the latent phase
A multipara who has not entered the active phase by 14 hours after the onset of the latent phase

questions.stem: All of the following findings are seen in the partogram of a patient except:
questions.explanation:
The above partogram shows secondary arrest of dilatation for >2 hour, arrest of descent for
>1 hour and a fall in fetal heart rate suggestive of fetal distress.
These are characteristic findings of obstructed labour and management is caesarean section.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old primigravida presents with labour pains. At 39 weeks of gestation, she was diagnosed with prolonged phase of labour. Which of the following is false regarding this condition? [[IMG:1]]
options: Excessive sedation can prolong this phase
questions.explanation:
The given clinical features suggest that the patient is in latent phase of labor. Latent phase is said to be prolonged if it is:
>20 h in nullipara
>14 h in multipara
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
Causes of prolonged latent phase:
Excessive sedation/epidural analgesia
Poor cervical conditions (thick, uneffaced)
False labour (most common cause in multipara)
Friedman's curve is used in the diagnosis of prolonged labour. It is the sigmoid curve plotting the pattern of cervical dilatation during the latent and active phase of normal labour.
Management includes morphine administration, rest and oxytocin stimulation.

questions.stem: Protracted active phase dilatation in a multiparous woman is when cervical dilatation is .
questions.explanation:
Protracted active phase dilatation in a multiparous woman is when cervical dilatation is less than
1.5 cm/hour.

questions.stem: Which among the following is false with respect to active phase of labor?
options: The minimum rate of cervical dilatation is 1.2cm/hr in nullipara
Arrest of dilatation is cessation of dilatation for >2 hours
Arrest of descent is cessation of descent for >1 hour
Poor cervical dilatation causes prolonged active phase
questions.explanation:
Poor cervical dilatation causes a prolonged latent phase.
Arrest of cervical dilatation is defined as the lack of cervical dilatation for  2 hours during the active phase of labour.
According to the Obstetric Care Consensus Committee, when cervical dilatation has reached  6 cm with ruptured membranes, and there is no cervical change despite 4 hours of adequate uterine contractions or 6 hours of inadequate contractions, a cesarean delivery is warranted.

questions.stem: Protracted descent in labor in a nullipara is
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
The protracted descent in labor in a nullipara is less than 1 cm/hour.

questions.stem: A multigravida is posted for C-section due to arrest of descent in labor. It is defined as no descent for [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation: Arrest of descent in labor in a multigravida is no descent for more than 1 hour.

questions.stem: What is the technique of stimulating uterine contractions in a pregnant patient prior to the onset of spontaneous labour known as? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The technique of stimulating uterine contractions prior to the onset of spontaneous labor is known as induction of labor.
It can be done irrespective of the rupture of membranes.
Augmentation is the enhancement of spontaneous contractions that are considered inadequate because of failed cervical dilation and fetal descent.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a contraindication for the induction of labor?
options: History of lower transverse cesarean section in last three pregnancies
questions.explanation: Heart disease is currently not considered a contraindication for the induction of labor. Vaginal delivery is preferred in such patients.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old G3P2 woman was admitted to the ward at 40 weeks of gestation for induction of labor. You were asked to calculate her Bishop's score. What should be the minimum score before performing this procedure?
questions.explanation:
The minimum Bishop Score required before proceeding with induction of labour is 6.
A Bishop score >8 conveys a high likelihood of a successful induction. The latest guidelines state that a cut-off score of 6 can be used to choose between pharmacological and mechanical methods of induction.
[[IMG:1]]
This score is calculated based on the:
station of the fetal head
dilation of cervix
cervical length
position of cervix
consistency of the cervix.
This score is an important determinant of a successful induction.

questions.stem: During rounds in the postnatal ward, you notice a patient's case sheet mentioning she had uterine tachysystole following labor induction. What is the criteria for this diagnosis?
options: More than 5 contractions in a 5-min period
More than 5 contractions in a 10-min period
More than 10 contractions in a 5-min period
More than 10 contractions in a 10-min period
questions.explanation:
Uterine tachysystole is defined as >5 contractions in a 10 min period and may occur in spontaneous or stimulated labor. It should always be qualified by the presence or absence of fetal heart rate abnormalities. Tachysystole interrupts maternal blood flow to the placenta during contractions and may lead to a reduction in fetal oxygenation. It is also associated with placental abruption.
It is caused by pharmacological agents used for cervical ripening and induction such as misoprostol (both oral and vaginal) and dinoprostone. Management includes stopping oxytocin infusion and terbutaline 0.25 mg SC.

questions.stem: A primigravida was admitted to the labor room at 41 weeks of gestation for the induction of labor. What is the dose of misoprostol used for this procedure? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
Misoprostol (PGE1) is given as 25mcg 3-6 hourly vaginally or 25mcg 2 hourly orally for the induction of labor.
It is associated with the following side effects:
Uterine tachysystole
Meconium stained amniotic fluid
Uterine rupture

questions.stem: Oxytocin is being given for augmentation of labour in a multigravida admitted to the labour room. Which of the following is not a mechanism of action of this drug?
options: Receptor mediation through G-protein coupled receptors
Activation of voltage mediated Ca channel
questions.explanation:
Competitive blocking of acetylcholine is not a mechanism of action of oxytocin. Mechanism of action of oxytocin is as follows:
Receptor mediation through G protein-coupled receptors
Activation of voltage-gated Ca channel leading to calcium entry
Prostaglandin production by a positive feedback mechanism. This induces production of more prostaglandins and stronger contractions.
[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: In which of the following patients would you perform a controlled artificial rupture of membranes?
options: G3P2 lady with absent fetal cardiac activity at 34 weeks of gestation
Multigravida with HIV at 36 weeks of gestation
G2P1 lady with AFI of 28 cm at 38 weeks of gestation
Term primigravida with red, tender, vesicular lesions on her vulva
questions.explanation:
Controlled artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) is performed in a patient with amniotic fluid index (AFI)  25 cm. This points towards a diagnosis of polyhydramnios.
This is because if ARM is not done under controlled conditions in these patients, it can cause sudden decompression of the fetus. This can lead to abruption of placenta.
Contraindications to ARM:
Intrauterine fetal death
Active genital herpes infection
Maternal HIV-AIDS

questions.stem: An obstetrician performs the following procedure for labor induction in a patient. Which of the following is false about the reflex elicited here? [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]]
options: Occurs due to pressure at the external os of cervix
It is associated with increased level of PGF2
Artificial rupture of membranes initiates this reflex
It is an example of positive feedback mechanism
questions.explanation:
Stripping of membranes is being depicted in the image, which elicits the Ferguson reflex. It is also known as the fetal ejection reflex and is seen due to the pressure at the internal os of the cervix.
It is associated with an increase in blood levels of a prostaglandin F2 metabolite, also known as dinoprost. This is released due to mechanical stretching of the internal os. This enhances the uterine activity and causes release of more prostaglandins. It is an example of a positive feedback mechanism.

questions.stem: All of the following are true about laminaria tents except:
options: Leads to the release of endogenous prostaglandins
questions.explanation:
The Bishop's score is rapidly improved by the use of laminaria tents.
It is a mechanical cervical dilator and acts by hygroscopic osmotic action, leading to slow dilatation of the cervix. The gentle dilatation by laminaria tents induces an endogenous synthesis of prostaglandins causing a softening of the cervix. This is useful in cervical ripening before induction of labour.

questions.stem: A nursing assistant posted in the obstetric care unit was asked to plot a partograph to monitor the progress of labour. Where should she start marking the cervical dilatation?
questions.explanation: In a partograph, the first marking of cervical dilatation should be made on the left of the alert line. In a normal partograph, the plotting remains on the left of the alert line.

questions.stem: You are monitoring the number, duration, and intensity of uterine contractions in a 34-year-old G2P1 woman with a term pregnancy. How long should they last for you to classify them as moderate? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
Moderate uterine contractions last for 20–40 s.
Weak contractions last for <20 s and strong contractions are >40 s.
During active labour, uterine contractions are 5 min apart for 1 hour, i.e.,  12 contractions in 1 hour. This is accompanied by cervical dilatation of 3–5 cm.
[[IMG:4]]

questions.stem: A G2P1 woman with polyhydramnios, presents to the clinic with respiratory distress at 38 weeks of gestation. The obstetrician plans for induction of labor. What is a safe method of induction in this patient?
options: Abdominal amniocentesis followed by oxytocin drip
questions.explanation:
Abdominal amniocentesis followed by oxytocin drip is a safe method for induction of labor in polyhydramnios.
Abdominal amniocentesis drains a good amount of liquor (amnioreduction), after which the oxytocin infusion can be started. This will minimize the sudden decompression and reduce the risk of placental separation, cord prolapse and change in lie of the fetus.
[[IMG:1]]
Although polyhydramnios does not constitute an absolute contraindication for the application of prostaglandins, these substances should be administered with caution. There is a marked increase in the incidence of postpartum hemorrhage and amniotic fluid embolism with their use.
Hence, amnioreduction is a preferred mode of treatment in polyhydramnios.

questions.stem: Given below is the partograph of a primigravida in labor. What should be the next step in managing her condition? [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]]
options: Induction of labor by mechanical methods
questions.explanation: As the plotting on the above partograph has crossed the action line, the next step of management is Caesarean section.

questions.stem: What is the half-life of oxytocin?
questions.explanation: The half-life of oxytocin is approximately 3–5 min. Therefore, once oxytocin infusion is stopped, its concentration in plasma rapidly falls.

questions.stem: During your OBG rotations, one of the senior residents asks you to induce labor in a primigravida admitted at 40 weeks of gestation. Identify the following device that you will use for the same. [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]]
questions.explanation:
This is an image of a cervidil vaginal insert. It is used for cervical ripening and improves the Bishop's score.
It contains 10 mg of dinoprostone designed to release at a rate of approximately 0.3 mg/hr over 10-hours.

questions.stem: According to the WHO Labour Care Guidelines, documentation of labour progress begins at a cervical dilatation of -
questions.explanation:
According to the WHO Labour Care Guidelines, documentation of labour progress begins at a cervical dilatation of 5cm.
WHO Labour Care Guidelines:
Time axis - examination findings are plotted every one hour
Alert column- has values which if reached indicates the need for urgent medical intervention
Active first stage - findings are plotted every hour upto 12 hours. If the first stage continues, a new sheet is used.
Second stage - plotted every hour upto 3 hours
Section 1: Preliminary information
Name, parity, labour onset, active labour diagnosis (date), ruptured membranes (date&time),
risk factors
Section 2: Supportive care
Companionship
[[IMG:1]]
Pain relief
Oral fluid
Posture
Section 3: Baby
Baseline FHR
FHR deceleration
Amniotic fluid
Fetal position
Caput
Moulding
Section 4: Vitals
